title: Sudden right upper quadrant pain after a barbecue lunch
desc: This station involves a focused history and abdominal examination of a 47-year-old teacher with sudden right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal, then interpreting her observations, bloods with a cholestatic liver function pattern and an ultrasound report, giving the diagnosis and differentials, outlining management in the emergency department, explaining the risk factors for gallstones and safety-netting.
focus: Acute right upper quadrant pain: telling acute cholecystitis apart from the rest of gallstone disease and reading a cholestatic LFT pattern
stem: You are the junior doctor in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital on a Sunday evening. Sally Sergeant, a 47-year-old primary school teacher, has come in with abdominal pain. Her husband drove her to the hospital. The triage nurse has taken her observations, put in an IV cannula and sent bloods. The nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from Sally and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, her blood results and an ultrasound report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting, and answer the examiner's questions (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Sally Sergeant, a 47-year-old primary school teacher. You are in a lot of pain, lying still on the trolley, flushed and sweaty. You are frightened because you have never felt pain like this. Answer clearly, but only give details when you are asked. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I have no idea what's happened, I'm usually pretty well but suddenly I have this pain!"

The pain (give only when asked)

  • Site: point under your ribs on the right.
  • Onset: it came on suddenly yesterday (Saturday) at about 4 pm, so about 26 hours ago.
  • What you were doing or ate before it started (if asked): "We had a big barbecue lunch at a friend's place yesterday at about 1 pm: roasts, sausages and chips."
  • Character: an intense, dull ache.
  • Radiation: if asked whether it goes anywhere: "I don't think so." Only if asked specifically about the shoulder or back: "I think I have some pain in my right shoulder, not sure if that's related."
  • Time course: constant since it started. It did not settle overnight and it has been getting worse. It does not come and go in waves.
  • Exacerbating and relieving: "I took a Panadol this afternoon and lay down with a heat pack, I don't think that helped much… Oh, it hurts more when I press on it."
  • Severity: "It was about a 5 out of 10 when it started yesterday. I thought it would settle overnight, but it didn't. It's been there the whole time and getting worse, and now it's an 8. This afternoon I started feeling hot and sweaty, and that really frightened me, so I asked Ron to drive me in." "I have never experienced anything so horrible."

Associated symptoms (only when asked)

  • You vomited once yesterday, about an hour after the pain started. It was food. There was no blood in it.
  • You have had no appetite at all since yesterday.
  • You are not sure whether you have had a fever, but since this afternoon you have felt hot and sweaty. No chills, no shaking (rigors).
  • Previous episodes: over the past year you have had a few episodes of discomfort in the same place, probably after meals. They were much milder and settled by themselves within a few hours, so you never saw anyone about them.

Negatives (only if asked about each)

  • No yellowing of the skin or eyes, no pale stools, no dark urine, no itch.
  • No pain in the upper middle of the tummy going through to the back.
  • No diarrhoea. You opened your bowels normally this morning and are passing wind. Your tummy is not swollen. You have not heard of anyone else from the barbecue being unwell.
  • No heartburn or reflux, no black stools, no vomiting blood. You do not take anti-inflammatories.
  • No chest pain, no breathlessness, no palpitations, no cough.
  • No pain or burning on passing urine and no blood in the urine. No vaginal bleeding or discharge. You take the pill every day and your last withdrawal bleed was 2 weeks ago, so you do not think you could be pregnant.
  • No weight loss, no night sweats, no lumps.

Background (only when asked)

  • Past history: appendix out at 15. Your GP told you your cholesterol is a little high and advised you to lose some weight. Nothing else.
  • Medications: the oral contraceptive pill (Yaz). The Panadol today at about 4 pm. Nothing else, no supplements.
  • Allergies: none known.
  • Family history: your mother is 75; she has had a hysterectomy and her gallbladder taken out, and she has diabetes. You do not know about your father (your parents divorced). Your older sister is well. Your two children are well.
  • Social: you have never smoked. About 2 glasses of alcohol a month. You teach at a primary school. You walk your dog. You cook 2 or 3 nights a week and eat out the rest. You live with your husband Ron and your daughter Stephanie; your son has moved out. You have good support.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Idea: "I must have had something dodgy at lunch yesterday. We had a big barbeque feast at a friend's house with all kinds of roasts and fries. I knew the sausages were a bit undercooked!"
  • Concern: "I really can't afford much time off work. It's Monday tomorrow and I have to take my classes on a camping trip. Do you think I can make it?" (Ask this in Part 1 if the candidate asks about your worries, or near the end of the history.)
  • Expectation: something to settle the pain so you can go home tonight.

Nurse and response to management

  • If asked for observations, the nurse gives the triage set: RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, BP 128/78, HR 104 regular, temperature 38.6 °C, alert, pain 8/10, BGL 6.1 mmol/L.
  • If the candidate arranges analgesia, the nurse gives it; about 10 minutes later Sally says the pain has eased to about 6/10, but the right upper abdomen is still very tender to touch.
  • If asked for a bedside ECG: sinus tachycardia 104/min, no ST or T wave changes.
  • If asked for a urine dipstick: negative for blood, leucocytes, nitrites and bilirubin.
  • If the candidate asks for blood results or imaging, say they will be given in Part 2.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: uncomfortable, lying still and avoiding movement, flushed and sweaty. Alert and oriented. Weight 88 kg, height 165 cm (BMI about 32).
  • Hands, eyes and skin: warm peripheries, CRT 2 seconds. Sclerae not yellow, no jaundice. No stigmata of chronic liver disease. Mucous membranes slightly dry.
  • Abdomen, inspection: not distended, moves with breathing; healed appendicectomy scar in the right iliac fossa. No visible masses.
  • Abdomen, palpation: marked tenderness in the right upper quadrant with voluntary guarding. Murphy's sign positive (she stops breathing in when the gallbladder area is pressed); no catch on the left. No tenderness elsewhere apart from mild epigastric discomfort. No rebound tenderness, no rigidity. No palpable gallbladder or mass. Liver not enlarged. Spleen and kidneys not palpable.
  • Percussion and auscultation: no percussion tenderness away from the right upper quadrant; no shifting dullness. Bowel sounds present and normal.
  • Renal angles: not tender. Hernial orifices: normal.
  • Chest: equal expansion, resonant, clear breath sounds including the right base. Heart: dual heart sounds, no murmurs.
  • Rectal or pelvic examination: if offered, the examiner says it is not needed.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self, confirms Sally's identity and gains consent before examining.
Recognises she is in severe pain: acknowledges it with empathy and asks the nurse for analgesia early instead of finishing the whole history first; uses plain language.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and onset: under the right ribs, started yesterday at about 4 pm after the barbecue, constant since (about 26 hours)
Character, severity and course: intense dull ache, started at about 5/10 and now 8/10, did not settle overnight, getting worse (constant, not settling within hours)
Radiation: asks specifically and elicits the right shoulder pain
Modifying factors: worse when pressed; Panadol and a heat pack did not help

check.x: Asks about associated symptoms: vomited once (food, no blood), anorexia, feels hot and sweaty since this afternoon, no chills or rigors.
Elicits the past year of milder right upper quadrant episodes after meals and links today's pain to the large fatty barbecue lunch.
Asks about biliary obstruction and cholangitis: jaundice, pale stools, dark urine and itch (all absent).
Screens for the other causes:

kids.x: Pancreatitis and peptic ulcer: epigastric pain through to the back, alcohol, NSAIDs, reflux, haematemesis, melaena
Gastroenteritis and bowel obstruction: diarrhoea, unwell contacts, bowels opening and passing wind, distension
Cardiorespiratory: chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations, cough (ACS, right lower lobe pneumonia)
Urinary, gynaecological and constitutional: urinary symptoms, last bleed and chance of pregnancy, weight loss, night sweats

check.x: Takes the past history, medications and allergies: appendicectomy at 15, mildly high cholesterol with advice to lose weight, the combined oral contraceptive pill (Yaz), no known drug allergies.
Takes the family history: mother had a cholecystectomy and has diabetes; father unknown; sister and children well.
Takes the social history: never smoked, about 2 drinks a month, primary school teacher, eats out most nights, walks her dog, lives with husband Ron and daughter Stephanie, good support.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: she thinks it is food poisoning from undercooked sausages and is worried about taking her class camping tomorrow.
Examination

General inspection and vital signs: notes she looks unwell, lies still, is flushed and sweaty; asks for the full set of observations; checks the sclerae and skin for jaundice (none) and assesses hydration.
Palpates the abdomen systematically, starting away from the pain, finds right upper quadrant tenderness with guarding and elicits a positive Murphy's sign.
check.d: Credit, but do not require, checking for the catch on the left side.

check.x: Looks for peritonitis and other causes: rebound or percussion tenderness, bowel sounds, liver edge and a palpable gallbladder, the appendicectomy scar, renal angles and hernial orifices.
Auscultates the chest, including the right base, and the heart; asks for a bedside ECG and urine dipstick and reviews the BGL.
Interpretation
Interprets the observations: temperature 38.6 rising to 38.9 °C in the yellow zone; HR 104 to 108 raised but in the white zone with normal BP: febrile, not shocked.
check.d: Credit, but do not require, noting that severe uncontrolled pain (8/10) meets the yellow-zone additional criteria and calls for a clinical review.

check.x: Interprets the WCC of 14.2 with neutrophilia and the CRP of 96 as acute inflammation, consistent with cholecystitis.
Interprets the liver function tests:
check.d: Credit Mirizzi and normal synthetic function (INR, albumin) if mentioned; do not require them.

kids.x: Cholestatic (obstructive) pattern: ALP 465 and GGT 205, more than 4 times the upper limit, with normal ALT/AST
The rise is more than a cystic duct block alone explains, so a CBD stone must be excluded

check.x: Notes the normal lipase (pancreatitis unlikely) and negative beta-hCG.
check.d: Credit normal renal function and coagulation.

check.x: Interprets the ultrasound as acute calculous cholecystitis (wall 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid, gallstones with one impacted in the neck, sonographic Murphy's sign) with a common bile duct of 5 mm that is not dilated.

Gives acute calculous cholecystitis as the most likely diagnosis, justified from the history, examination and results, and gives the differentials with a feature for or against each: choledocholithiasis or cholangitis (kept open, not excluded: fever with cholestatic LFTs, so the duct needs imaging; credit, but do not require, noting that this meets TG18 suspected cholangitis), biliary colic, acute pancreatitis, and at least one of peptic ulcer, right lower lobe pneumonia or ACS.
Management
Analgesia (titrated IV opioid + antiemetic, regular paracetamol timed from 16:00), nil by mouth, IV crystalloid, blood cultures before antibiotics.
Starts IV antibiotics per eTG: amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 4 to 7 mg/kg IV (adjusted body weight) as a single dose, with the dosing interval set by renal function.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: empirical gentamicin for no more than 72 hours; ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily if gentamicin is contraindicated; adjusting to severity and local guidance.

check.x: Refers to the general surgical team for admission and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this admission.
Plans assessment for a duct stone (MRCP before surgery or an intraoperative cholangiogram), with ERCP if a stone is found.
check.d: Credit repeat LFTs and VTE prophylaxis (enoxaparin 40 mg subcut daily) if mentioned, but do not require them.

check.x: Safety netting
Explains in plain words at least 3 of Sally's own risk factors for gallstones: being a woman, her age (47), her weight (BMI 32), the combined pill (Yaz), and her mother's gallbladder operation.
check.d: Raised cholesterol may be credited alongside her weight. The general causes (cholesterol and pigment stones) are in the explanation and are credited but not required.

check.x: Explains to Sally in plain words that a gallstone has blocked and inflamed her gallbladder (not food poisoning), that she needs to stay in hospital, and that she cannot go on the camping trip; does not send her home.
check.d: Credit, but do not require, offering a medical certificate and offering to call Ron.

check.x: Tells Sally to press the call bell at once for at least 2 of: shaking chills, yellow eyes or skin, worse or spreading pain.
Asks the nurse for at least hourly observations and to escalate a falling BP, rising HR, new confusion or any red-zone value (rapid response).

part2.lead: Here are Sally's observations, her blood results and the ultrasound report.
part2.patient:
Question 4 opens with Sally's own questions. React to the answer:

  • If told she cannot go camping, be disappointed: "But who's going to take them?" Accept it if the candidate explains kindly why she must stay (an offer of a medical certificate helps).
  • If the candidate uses jargon (cholecystitis, laparoscopic, ERCP, MRCP), ask: "What does that mean?"
  • If asked, you are happy for them to call Ron.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Triage set at 18:05 and the nurse's repeat set at 18:50, both on room air. She took paracetamol at home at about 16:00.
handover.model:
• Read: at triage the temperature of 38.6 °C is in the yellow zone, and severe uncontrolled pain (8/10) meets the yellow-zone additional criteria; HR 104, BP 128/78, RR 18 and SpO2 97% on room air are white. At 18:50 the temperature has risen to 38.9 °C (still yellow) and HR to 108 (white), BP 122/74; pain 6/10 if analgesia given (8/10 if not), RUQ still tender.
  • Meaning: a fever that is rising despite paracetamol at 16:00, with tachycardia, is a systemic inflammatory response to infection or inflammation. She is not shocked and nothing is in the red zone.
  • Changes: the yellow zone calls for a clinical review within 30 minutes (this review) and more frequent observations. Screen for sepsis (blood cultures before antibiotics, lactate) and escalate to a rapid response if any value enters the red zone.

rows.note: Triage ATS 3: severe RUQ pain; IV cannula, bloods sent

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Sally Sergeant, DOB 01/05/1979. Collected 18:10, Sunday. Sample not haemolysed.
handover.model:
• Read: WCC 14.2 with neutrophils 11.6 and CRP 96: acute inflammation. ALP 465 and GGT 205, more than 4 times the upper limit, with bilirubin only slightly raised at 26: a cholestatic (obstructive) pattern. ALT, AST and albumin are normal. Lipase, UEC, coagulation and Hb are normal; beta-hCG is negative. Normal lactate: no hypoperfusion.
  • Meaning: a blocked cystic duct alone usually causes only mild LFT changes; ALP and GGT more than 4x ULN raise the possibility of a CBD stone (small, passed, or in the distal duct the scan did not see) or, less likely, Mirizzi compression. The slight bilirubin rise and 5 mm duct make complete CBD obstruction unlikely but do not exclude a stone. Fever with these LFTs meets TG18 criteria for suspected cholangitis, so a duct stone has to be looked for. The normal transaminases mean no hepatocellular injury, and the normal albumin and INR mean normal synthetic function. With the history and the inflammatory markers, this is cholecystitis. The normal lipase makes pancreatitis unlikely, and she is not pregnant, which matters for imaging, drugs and theatre.
  • Changes: the results support IV antibiotics and surgical admission. Because the LFTs are abnormal, plan assessment for a duct stone now (MRCP before surgery, or an intraoperative cholangiogram at laparoscopic cholecystectomy), with ERCP if a stone is confirmed; repeat the LFTs in 24 hours.

handover.label: Ultrasound of the upper abdomen
handover.result:
Examination: ultrasound of the upper abdomen (liver, gallbladder, biliary tree, pancreas, right kidney), 20:10.

Clinical details: 47-year-old woman, sudden constant right upper quadrant pain for about 28 hours radiating to the right shoulder, fever 38.9 °C, Murphy's sign positive. WCC 14.2, CRP 96, ALP 465, bilirubin 26. ?Acute cholecystitis.

Findings:

  • Gallbladder: distended. Wall diffusely thickened to 5 mm and oedematous, with a small rim of pericholecystic fluid. Multiple mobile gallstones up to 18 mm with posterior acoustic shadowing. A 15 mm stone is impacted in the gallbladder neck and does not move when the patient changes position. Positive sonographic Murphy's sign. No gas in the wall, no wall defect and no collection.
  • Bile ducts: common bile duct 5 mm at the porta hepatis. No intrahepatic duct dilatation. No stone seen in the visualised duct; the distal common bile duct is partly obscured by bowel gas.
  • Liver: normal size and echotexture. No focal lesion.
  • Pancreas: head and body normal; tail obscured by bowel gas. No peripancreatic fluid.
  • Right kidney: normal size, no hydronephrosis, no calculus.
  • Other: no free fluid in the abdomen.

Conclusion: acute calculous cholecystitis with a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck. Common bile duct not dilated; no duct stone seen, although the distal duct is not fully seen.
handover.model:
• Read: the gallbladder is distended, with a thickened wall (5 mm; 4 mm or more is thickened, TG18), pericholecystic fluid, multiple stones, one impacted in the neck, and a positive sonographic Murphy's sign. There is no gas in the wall, no perforation and no collection. The common bile duct is 5 mm with no intrahepatic dilatation; the distal duct is not fully seen.
  • Meaning: this confirms acute calculous cholecystitis caused by the impacted neck stone. The neck stone alone does not explain ALP and GGT more than 4 times the upper limit: with the distal duct not fully seen, a common bile duct stone, or Mirizzi compression of the common hepatic duct by the neck stone, is not excluded. No intrahepatic duct dilatation makes Mirizzi less likely; a small or passed CBD stone is the main concern. A non-dilated duct makes complete duct obstruction unlikely but does not exclude a stone. With no complication on the scan and a WCC below 18, the cholecystitis is mild (Tokyo Grade I).
  • Changes: admit under general surgery for IV antibiotics and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Because the LFTs are abnormal and the distal duct was not seen, assess for a duct stone now (MRCP before surgery, or an intraoperative cholangiogram at laparoscopic cholecystectomy), with ERCP if a stone is confirmed.

ask: You are now calling the general surgical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Sally Sergeant, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Sally now, here in the emergency department.
Sally asks you, "Why did I get gallstones, and can I still take my class camping tomorrow?" Please answer her, then tell me what you would ask the nurse to watch for.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED junior doctor; Sally Sergeant, 47.
  • Situation: acute calculous cholecystitis; febrile, Murphy's positive; requesting surgical admission.
  • Background: sudden constant RUQ pain since about 16:00 yesterday after a fatty barbecue lunch, radiating to the right shoulder, vomited once; a year of milder postprandial episodes; appendicectomy, high cholesterol, BMI 32, combined OCP, no known drug allergies; mother had a cholecystectomy.
  • Assessment: T 38.6 rising to 38.9 °C (yellow zone), HR 108, BP normal, not shocked; WCC 14.2, CRP 96 inflammatory; ALP 465 and GGT 205 with bilirubin 26, normal ALT/AST: cholestatic, more than a cystic duct block explains, possible duct stone; lipase normal, hCG negative; ultrasound: wall 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid, impacted neck stone, CBD 5 mm, distal duct not seen.
  • Recommendation: analgesia, fluids, cultures and IV antibiotics started; please review for admission, early laparoscopic cholecystectomy and duct assessment (MRCP or intraoperative cholangiogram).

Acute calculous cholecystitis: constant RUQ pain for over a day after a fatty meal, right shoulder radiation, fever, previous postprandial episodes, Murphy's sign, WCC and CRP raised, thick-walled gallbladder with an impacted neck stone.

  • Choledocholithiasis or cholangitis: for: fever, WCC and CRP raised, ALP and GGT more than 4x ULN (meets TG18 suspected cholangitis); against: no clinical jaundice, bilirubin only 26, CBD 5 mm with no intrahepatic dilatation, not septic. Needs duct imaging (MRCP or intraoperative cholangiogram) to exclude.
  • Biliary colic: for: past episodes; against: constant pain, fever, inflammatory markers, wall thickening.
  • Acute pancreatitis: against: normal lipase, pain not epigastric to back, little alcohol.
  • Peptic ulcer, right lower lobe pneumonia, ACS: against: no NSAIDs or reflux, chest clear, no chest symptoms (and normal ECG if obtained). Not gastroenteritis (no diarrhoea); appendix already removed.

1. Titrated IV opioid with an antiemetic, regular paracetamol; nil by mouth, IV crystalloid, blood cultures before antibiotics.
  2. IV antibiotics per eTG: amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 4 to 7 mg/kg IV (adjusted body weight) single dose, interval by renal function.
  3. General surgery: admit for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
  4. Duct assessment: MRCP or intraoperative cholangiogram, ERCP if a stone is found.

• Why: at least 3 of her own risk factors in plain words: a woman, age 47, her weight, the combined pill, her mother's gallbladder operation.
  • Camping: a stone has blocked and inflamed her gallbladder (not food poisoning); she needs to stay in hospital and will likely have it removed this admission, so no camping trip (credit a medical certificate, calling Ron).
  • Call bell at once for shaking chills, yellow eyes or skin, worse or spreading pain.
  • Nurse: at least hourly observations; escalate a falling BP, rising HR, confusion or any red-zone value (rapid response).

guide:
In Part 1, Sally gives each part of the history only when asked. She mentions the shoulder pain only if asked specifically about radiation to the shoulder or back. The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate asks for blood results or imaging in Part 1, say they will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over the observations, bloods and ultrasound report, then ask the four questions in order. Question 4 opens with Sally's own questions (why gallstones, and the camping trip); she does not raise them during the management answer.

Observations: if no analgesia was ordered in Part 1, read pain as 8/10 at 18:50.

A high-performing candidate arranges analgesia early. They characterise constant right upper quadrant pain for over a day with right shoulder radiation, elicit the fever, the vomiting and the previous postprandial episodes, and screen for jaundice and the other differentials. They elicit Murphy's sign and check for jaundice and peritonitis. In Part 2 they read the LFTs as cholestatic, recognise that this degree of rise is more than a cystic duct block alone explains, and plan duct imaging, noting normal transaminases and synthetic function. They read the ultrasound as acute calculous cholecystitis with a non-dilated duct and manage with analgesia, fluids, cultures, IV antibiotics and surgical admission for early cholecystectomy. They tell Sally kindly that she cannot go on the camping trip, and they list the gallstone risk factors that apply to her.

A borderline candidate misses the jaundice questions or Murphy's sign, reads the LFTs only as "abnormal", or plans no duct assessment. A failing candidate calls it food poisoning or biliary colic and plans to send her home with analgesia.

Credit only, never required: noting that fever with these LFTs meets TG18 criteria for suspected cholangitis, and grading the cholecystitis as mild (Tokyo Grade I), whether in the ISBAR or the differentials.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute calculous cholecystitis

Sally has had sudden, constant right upper quadrant pain for more than a day after a large fatty meal. The pain radiates to the right shoulder (referred through the phrenic nerve from diaphragmatic irritation). She has fever, anorexia and a vomit, and a year of milder postprandial episodes that were probably biliary colic. On examination there is a positive Murphy's sign, a localising sign of peritoneal irritation over the inflamed gallbladder. The WCC and CRP are raised and the ultrasound shows a thick-walled gallbladder with an impacted neck stone. Under the Tokyo Guidelines (TG18) this is a definite diagnosis: local signs, systemic signs and confirming imaging. It is mild (Grade I): WCC below 18, no palpable mass, under 72 hours, no local complication and no organ dysfunction.

The spectrum of gallstone disease

  • Cholelithiasis: stones in the gallbladder. Up to 15% of Australians over 50 have gallstones, mostly without symptoms.
  • Biliary colic: a stone transiently blocks the cystic duct. Postprandial pain that settles within about 6 hours, with no fever and normal inflammatory markers.
  • Acute cholecystitis: the cystic duct stays blocked and the gallbladder becomes inflamed. Constant RUQ pain for hours, possibly referred to the right shoulder, with fever, Murphy's sign and raised WCC and CRP.
  • Choledocholithiasis: stones in the common bile duct, with cholestatic LFTs, jaundice, dark urine and pale stools.
  • Cholangitis: infection behind a blocked duct. Charcot's triad (RUQ pain, fever, jaundice), often with sepsis.

Reading the pain

Localised pain with tenderness and guarding means parietal peritoneal irritation (for example, Murphy's sign in cholecystitis, or tenderness at McBurney's point in appendicitis). Vague, generalised pain is visceral. Colicky pain comes from a hollow viscus contracting against an obstruction (bowel, ureter). Biliary "colic" is usually a steady pain that builds and settles within about 6 hours. What separates it from cholecystitis is duration, fever and local peritonism, not the waveform. Peritonitic pain with guarding and rigidity follows rupture.

Interpreting the LFTs

  • Cholestatic: ALP and GGT raised, often with a raised bilirubin; the transaminases rise mildly if obstruction is prolonged, and an acutely impacted duct stone can cause an early transaminase spike.
  • Hepatitic: AST and ALT high, with a raised bilirubin and a raised INR (acute) or low albumin (chronic) when synthetic function fails.
  • Pre-hepatic: raised unconjugated bilirubin with normal enzymes, as in haemolysis or Gilbert syndrome.

Sally's ALP and GGT are more than 4 times the upper limit, with a bilirubin only slightly raised at 26. A blocked cystic duct alone leaves bile flowing from the liver, so it usually causes normal or only mildly abnormal LFTs. A rise this large points to obstruction of hepatic bile outflow: a common bile duct stone (small, already passed, or in the distal duct this scan did not fully see), or, less likely here because the intrahepatic ducts are not dilated, a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck pressing on the common hepatic duct (Mirizzi syndrome). In partial or intermittent duct obstruction, ALP and GGT are often raised while the bilirubin is normal or only slightly raised, so a bilirubin of 26 and a 5 mm duct make complete obstruction unlikely but do not exclude a stone. Fever with ALP and GGT over 1.5 times the upper limit also meets TG18 criteria for suspected acute cholangitis (systemic inflammation plus cholestasis). Abnormal liver tests put her at least at intermediate risk of a duct stone (ASGE 2019), so the duct is assessed now: MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound before surgery, or an intraoperative cholangiogram at laparoscopic cholecystectomy, with ERCP for a confirmed stone. Normal transaminases mean no hepatocellular injury, and normal INR and albumin mean normal synthetic function. A normal lactate means there is no hypoperfusion.

Differentials that matter

Choledocholithiasis and cholangitis (kept open here until the duct is imaged), biliary colic, acute pancreatitis (excluded here by a normal lipase and the pain pattern), peptic ulcer disease and GORD, acalculous cholecystitis (usually in critically ill patients), gallbladder polyps or cancer, sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, liver abscess, right lower lobe pneumonia and ACS. Appendicitis is off the list because her appendix was removed at 15. Her own idea of food poisoning does not fit: there is no diarrhoea, the pain is localised, and there are signs of peritoneal irritation.

Management

  • Analgesia (titrated IV opioid and an antiemetic, plus paracetamol), nil by mouth and IV fluids.
  • Blood cultures, then IV antibiotics for acute cholecystitis as eTG recommends: amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 4 to 7 mg/kg IV (adjusted body weight in obesity; her BMI is 32) for 1 dose, then dosing interval by renal function; empirical gentamicin for no more than 72 hours; if gentamicin is contraindicated, ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily; adjusted to severity and local guidance.
  • Admission under the general surgical team for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission. Interval surgery after recovery risks recurrence and complications.
  • Assessment for a duct stone, because the LFTs are abnormal and the distal duct was not seen: MRCP (or endoscopic ultrasound) before surgery, or an intraoperative cholangiogram at cholecystectomy, with ERCP if a stone is confirmed. LFTs are repeated in 24 hours.
  • ICU review if there is organ dysfunction.
  • VTE prophylaxis (enoxaparin 40 mg subcut daily), because emergency surgery, obesity and the combined OCP all add to her risk. Her contraception is reviewed after surgery.

Cholangitis is managed differently. It needs IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within the hour if she is septic (Sepsis Clinical Care Standard), fluid boluses and urgent biliary decompression by ERCP.

Complications of cholecystitis and gallstones include empyema, gangrene or perforation of the gallbladder, gallstone ileus, pancreatitis, cholangitis and liver abscess.

Gallstone risk factors

Cholesterol stones are the most common. Risk factors are female sex, obesity and the metabolic syndrome, family history, oestrogen (the OCP, HRT and the fertile years), pregnancy, rapid weight loss or prolonged fasting, diabetes, and drugs such as fibrates and somatostatin analogues.

Pigment stones follow haemolysis, biliary infection, cirrhosis, and Crohn's disease or ileal resection.

Ceftriaxone can cause biliary sludge (calcium–ceftriaxone pseudolithiasis).

Sally has several cholesterol stone risks: she is a 47-year-old woman, obese (BMI 32) with a raised cholesterol, taking a combined OCP, and her mother had a cholecystectomy.

Safety netting

Sally cannot take her class on the camping trip: she needs admission under the surgical team. While she is in hospital, the nurse escalates rigors, rising fever, jaundice, worsening or spreading pain, a rigid abdomen, a falling BP, a rising HR or confusion. These suggest cholangitis, perforation or sepsis. After the operation she sees her GP within 1 to 2 weeks to check the wound and the histology and to review her weight, cholesterol and contraception. She returns to the ED for fever, jaundice, worsening pain or a red, discharging wound.
points: Biliary colic is postprandial pain that settles within about 6 hours. Constant RUQ pain for hours, with fever, Murphy's sign and raised WCC and CRP, is acute cholecystitis.

A blocked cystic duct alone usually causes only mild LFT changes. ALP and GGT more than 4 times the upper limit suggest a common bile duct stone, so plan duct imaging. In partial or intermittent duct obstruction, ALP and GGT are often raised while the bilirubin is normal or only slightly raised, so a bilirubin of 26 and a 5 mm duct make complete obstruction unlikely but do not exclude a stone. Fever with these LFTs meets TG18 criteria for suspected cholangitis.

Ultrasound is the first test: wall 4 mm or more, distension, pericholecystic fluid, stones and a sonographic Murphy's sign. Abnormal LFTs or a duct that is not fully seen call for MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound before surgery, or an intraoperative cholangiogram, and ERCP for a confirmed duct stone.
Acute cholecystitis needs analgesia, IV fluids, blood cultures, IV antibiotics as eTG recommends, and admission for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy; it is not a discharge diagnosis.
Charcot's triad (RUQ pain, fever, jaundice) means cholangitis: antibiotics within the hour if septic, fluid resuscitation and urgent ERCP decompression.

Cholesterol stone risk factors include female sex, obesity, family history, oestrogen (OCP, HRT, fertile years), pregnancy, rapid weight loss and diabetes. Pigment stones follow haemolysis, biliary infection, cirrhosis and ileal disease.
